experiments.title: The Balloon Rocket
experiments.question: Which way does a balloon move when it lets its air out? Does more air send it further?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the air rushes out of the balloon's neck, will the balloon go the same way as the air, or the opposite way? Will a balloon with 9 breaths go further than one with 3 breaths? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the number of breaths: 3, then 6, then 9. Use the same balloon, the same string and the same starting place. Try each one 2 or 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a balloon, round or long
a smooth string, such as nylon string, about 4 metres long, or as long as your room allows. Never use kite manja, which has glass on it.
a drinking straw
sticky tape
two chairs
a measuring tape (a tailor's tape works)

experiments.safety: Do not let small children chew balloons. Throw away burst balloon pieces at once. A grown-up blows up the balloon if the child finds it hard.

schedule.what: Build the balloon rocket. Test 3, 6 and 9 breaths. Measure how far it goes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the balloon with two arrows: one for the air pushed out backwards, and one for the push on the balloon.

setup.art: A long string threaded through a drinking straw and tied tightly between two chairs across a room.
setup.caption: 1. Thread the string through a straw. Tie it between two chairs.

setup.art: A blown-up long balloon held shut at the neck, being taped under the straw.
setup.caption: 2. Blow up the balloon. Hold the neck shut. Tape it under the straw.

setup.art: The balloon whooshing along the string, air rushing out of the neck behind it, a measuring tape on the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Let go. Measure how far it goes along the string.

flow.do: 1. Thread the string through the straw. 2. Tie each end of the string to a chair. 3. Pull the chairs apart until the string is tight.
flow.say: This string is the rocket's track. The straw will slide along it, carrying our balloon rocket.
flow.kid: Thread the string through the straw. Tie each end to a chair. Pull the chairs apart so the string is tight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Balloon Rocket experiment. You build a track for a balloon to fly along.

flow.do: 1. Blow 3 breaths into the balloon. 2. Pinch the neck shut. Do not tie it. 3. While one person pinches, the other tapes the balloon under the straw, with its neck pointing towards one chair. 4. Slide it to that chair.
flow.say: Three breaths only. Hold the neck shut. Which way will the air rush out? Which way will the balloon go? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Blow 3 breaths into the balloon. Pinch the neck. Tape it under the straw. Which way will it go?

ask.q: Which way will the balloon go when you let go?
good: The opposite way to the air.
Away from the neck.

flow.do: 1. Let go. 2. Measure from the start to where the straw stopped. 3. Write it down. If it reaches the end of the string, write 'reached the end'. 4. Repeat with 6 breaths and 9 breaths.
flow.say: Let go! How far did it go? Now let's try 6 breaths, then 9.
flow.kid: Let go! Measure how far it went. Write it down. Then try 6 breaths. Then try 9.

check.q: The air rushes out of the balloon's neck backwards. Which way does the balloon go?
options: Forwards, the opposite way to the air
check.why: The balloon pushes air backwards, and the air pushes the balloon forwards. Picking 'backwards' means the balloon was pictured being carried along with its air.

flow.parent: Ask for your child's answer to the check first. Then: the balloon squeezes the air and pushes it out backwards. The air pushes the balloon forwards just as hard. That forward push is called thrust. Real rockets work the same way, with hot gas instead of air. They do not need air outside to push against.

flow.do: Compare the three distances.
flow.say: Which went furthest? Why do you think more air made it go further?
flow.kid: Which balloon went furthest? Why do you think so?

chart.x: Breaths of air in the balloon

flow.think: Tipu Sultan's army in Mysore used iron rockets in battles more than 200 years ago. They also worked by pushing gas backwards. What do you think pushed them?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the balloon goes the opposite way to the air. What I saw: the air rushed out backwards and the balloon zoomed forwards. With 9 breaths it went much further than with 3. Why: the balloon pushes the air back, and the air pushes the balloon forward. More air means it pushes for longer.

experiments.title: Blow the Ball: does direction matter?
experiments.question: Does the direction of a push change which way a ball goes? What happens with two pushes at once?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you blow on a ping-pong ball from one side, which way will it go? If two people blow from opposite sides, equally hard? If they blow from two sides next to each other, such as the bottom and the left? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same ball and the same tray each time. Blow from about the same distance, about one hand-width away, and about as hard. Change only where you blow from.

materials.item: a ping-pong ball, or a scrunched ball of paper
two drinking straws
a large flat tray, a baking tray or a big sheet of paper with a square drawn on it
a pencil to draw arrows

experiments.safety: Each person uses their own straw. Stop and rest if you feel dizzy.

schedule.what: Blow the ball from one side, two opposite sides and two corner sides. Draw the arrows.

experiments.record: For each test, draw the tray from above. Draw an arrow for each blow and an arrow for the way the ball went.

setup.art: A ping-pong ball in the middle of a flat tray, seen from above, with a straw at the bottom edge.
setup.caption: 1. Put the ball in the middle of the tray.

setup.art: Two children blowing through straws from opposite edges of the tray, the ball staying in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Blow from opposite sides, equally hard.

setup.art: Two children blowing from the bottom edge and the left edge, the ball rolling towards the top right corner.
setup.caption: 3. Blow from two sides next to each other.

flow.do: 1. Put the ball in the middle of the tray. 2. Your child blows through a straw from the bottom edge of the tray, about one hand-width from the ball.
flow.say: Blow through your straw from this side. Which way does the ball go? Draw an arrow for your blow and an arrow for the ball.
flow.kid: Put the ball in the middle. Blow through the straw from one side. Which way does the ball go?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blow the Ball experiment. You push a ping-pong ball with your breath from different directions.

flow.do: 1. Put the ball back in the middle. 2. You and your child blow from opposite edges at the same moment, equally hard. 3. Then one of you blows harder.
flow.say: Let's both blow from opposite sides, equally hard. What happens? Now I'll blow harder. Now what?
flow.kid: Blow from opposite sides, both at once. Equally hard. What happens? Now one blows harder.

check.q: Two people blow on the ball from opposite sides, equally hard. What happens?
options: The ball races off one way
The ball stays about where it is, because the pushes balance
check.why: Equal pushes from opposite sides balance, so the ball stays about where it is. Picking 'races off' means one blow was pictured as stronger.

flow.do: 1. Put the ball back in the middle. 2. Your child blows from the bottom edge. You blow from the left edge. Blow at the same moment. 3. Watch the way the ball goes.
flow.say: Now one blow from the bottom and one from the side. Which way does it go now?
flow.kid: One blow from the bottom. One from the side. Blow together. Which way does the ball go?

ask.q: Why did the ball go slantwise, towards the corner?
good: One blow pushed it up and the other pushed it sideways.
The two pushes added up into a slanting push.

flow.parent: Two pushes at a corner add up to a slanting push, between the two. Scientists call this adding vectors. The ball goes towards the corner opposite both blowers. Do not worry if it is not exact. Breath is wobbly.

flow.do: Look at all the arrow drawings together.
flow.say: Look at your arrows. Was the push ever pointing one way while the ball went another?
flow.kid: Look at your arrows. Did the ball always go where the pushes pointed?

activities.title: Push and Pull Hunt, and the Mystery Bag

materials.item: a cloth bag with 8 to 10 small household things inside, like a peg, a key, a spoon, a ball, a rubber band, a zip pouch, a toy car and a jar with a lid
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Choose things with no sharp edges. Keep the hunt indoors, or go outside with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Pull things out of the mystery bag and find their forces. Then hunt for pushes and pulls at home.

activities.record: Draw three columns: PUSH, PULL and BOTH. Write each thing you found in the right column.

setup.art: A child's hand reaching into a cloth bag, a peg, a key and a toy car peeping out.
setup.caption: 1. Pull one thing out of the mystery bag.

setup.art: A child using a peg, squeezing it open, with a small arrow on each side.
setup.caption: 2. Use it. Feel the push or pull.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three columns labelled PUSH, PULL and BOTH, filling up with words.
setup.caption: 3. Write it in the right column.

flow.do: 1. Your child pulls one thing out of the bag without looking. 2. They use it the way it is meant to be used. 3. They say whether it needed a push, a pull or both.
flow.say: Pull something out of the bag. Use it. Did your hand push, pull or do both?
flow.kid: Pull one thing from the bag. Use it. Did you push, pull or both?

ask.q: A peg. Push, pull or both?
good: A push. I squeeze it.
Both. I squeeze it, and the spring snaps it shut again.

ask.q: A jar with a lid. What force opens it?
good: A twist.
Both. A push on one side and a pull on the other.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Push and Pull Hunt. Your child pulls things from a mystery bag and finds the push or pull each one needs.

flow.do: Walk round the home together for 10 minutes. Find at least 12 more pushes and pulls. Your child writes each one in a column.
flow.say: Now let's hunt the whole house. Door handles, switches, taps, zips, curtains. Find 12 forces.
flow.kid: Hunt the whole house. Find 12 pushes and pulls. Write each one in its column.
flow.parent: Expect these. Door handle and curtains are pulls. A light switch and a mixer button are pushes. A tap and a pressure cooker lid are twists, so both. A drawer is pulled out and pushed in.

flow.do: Count each column together.
flow.say: Which column is longest? Were there more pushes or pulls in our house?
flow.kid: Count each column. Which is longest?
flow.think: A drawer is pulled out and pushed in. Is it a push thing or a pull thing? Or is that the wrong question?

activities.context: This is a hunt for forces at home. It starts with a mystery bag of everyday things, and ends with a list of pushes and pulls from every room.

activities.title: Gentle Tug of War, with arrows

materials.item: a thick soft rope, or two old dupattas or sarees twisted together
a ribbon or cloth strip to mark the middle
a floor that does not slip, such as bare tiles for bare feet, with cushions behind each player
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Play barefoot on a floor that does not slip, with cushions behind each player, or on grass. Never wrap the rope round hands, wrists or necks. The grown-up pulls gently and never lets go suddenly.

schedule.what: Play three gentle rounds of tug of war. Try standing tall, then crouching low. Draw the arrows.

activities.record: Draw one round of the tug of war. Draw an arrow for each team's pull, and an arrow for the ground's push on each team's feet.

setup.art: A rope laid on a tiled floor with a ribbon tied in the middle and a strip of tape on the floor under the ribbon.
setup.caption: 1. Tie a ribbon on the middle of the rope. Mark a line under it.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up holding opposite ends, the child standing tall and the grown-up crouching low.
setup.caption: 2. Pull gently. First stand tall, then crouch low.

setup.art: A drawing of the tug of war with two long arrows along the rope and two short arrows under the feet.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the arrows.

flow.do: 1. Lay the rope on the floor. 2. Tie the ribbon on the middle. 3. Put a strip of tape or a stick on the floor under the ribbon. 4. Put cushions behind each player.
flow.say: This is a gentle tug of war. The ribbon shows the middle of the rope. If the ribbon crosses to your side, you win.
flow.kid: Fetch a grown-up. Tie a ribbon on the rope's middle. Mark a line under it. Pull the ribbon to your side to win.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Gentle Tug of War activity. You play a safe tug of war and then draw it with force arrows.

flow.do: 1. Round 1: both of you stand tall and pull with your arms only. 2. Round 2: your child crouches low, leans back and digs their heels in. Keep your own pull the same.
flow.say: First round, stand tall and pull with your arms. Second round, crouch low and push your heels into the floor. Which felt stronger? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Round 1: stand tall, pull with your arms. Round 2: crouch low. Push your heels into the ground. Which was stronger?

ask.q: Which way felt stronger, and why do you think so?
good: Crouching. My feet pushed the floor, and the floor pushed me back.
Crouching, because I could push the floor harder.

flow.parent: The rope pulls both of you equally hard. What changes is how hard each of you pushes the ground. Crouching low lets you push the ground towards the middle with your heels. The ground pushes you back, away from the middle.

flow.do: Round 3: hold the rope still between you, both pulling gently. Then palm to palm, push equally so nobody moves.
flow.say: Let's pull so that nobody moves. Now push palms, both equally. Are there forces, even though nothing moves?
flow.kid: Pull so nobody moves. Now push palms together equally. Is there a force, even with no moving?

check.q: In a tug of war, the rope is not moving. What is true?
options: Both sides are pulling equally, so the forces are balanced
The rope is too heavy to move
check.why: A still rope means both sides pull equally, so the forces are balanced. Picking 'nobody is pulling' means balanced was mixed up with no forces at all.

flow.do: Help your child draw the tug of war. For each person's pull on the rope, draw one arrow along the rope, pointing away from the middle. Draw one short arrow under each person's feet for the ground's push.
flow.say: Draw each pull as an arrow along the rope. Now, under each person, draw the ground pushing them back. Which way does that arrow point?
flow.kid: Draw each pull as an arrow on the rope. Under each person, draw the ground's push. Which way does it point?
flow.think: If the rope pulls both teams equally, what really decides who wins?

activities.context: This is a gentle tug of war between a child and a grown-up. Afterwards, you draw it with force arrows, including the push of the ground.

activities.title: The Bending Ruler: forces when nothing moves

materials.item: a thin plastic ruler
two tins or two piles of books of the same height
a small book or a steel tiffin box
a sponge

activities.safety: Use a plastic ruler, not glass. Press gently so it does not snap.

schedule.what: Bridge a ruler between two tins, rest a book on it, and see the hidden push.

activities.record: Draw the book on the ruler with two arrows: gravity pulling down and the ruler pushing up. Make them the same length.

setup.art: A thin plastic ruler resting across the tops of two tins, like a little bridge.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the ruler across two tins.

setup.art: A small book resting on the middle of the ruler, the ruler bending down in a gentle curve.
setup.caption: 2. Put a small book in the middle. Watch it bend.

setup.art: A book on a table with an arrow down labelled gravity and an arrow up labelled the table pushes up.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the two arrows.

flow.do: Point at a book lying still on the table.
flow.say: This book is not moving. Are there any forces on it?
flow.kid: Look at a book on the table. It is not moving. Are there any forces on it?

ask.q: Why doesn't the book fall through the table?
good: The table holds it up.
The table pushes up on it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Bending Ruler activity. You find the hidden forces on something that is not moving.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler across two tins like a bridge. 2. Put the small book in the middle. 3. Watch the ruler bend. 4. Take the book off and watch it spring back.
flow.say: Look how the ruler bends under the book. What do you think the bent ruler is doing to the book?
flow.kid: Lay the ruler across two tins. Put a book in the middle. See it bend? What is the ruler doing?
flow.parent: Wait for your child's idea. Then: the bent ruler pushes up on the book, and the table does the same, but it bends too little to see. This push from a surface is called the support force. Scientists also call it the normal force. When the book presses on the table, the table's atoms are squeezed a tiny bit closer together, and they push back.

flow.do: Your child presses a hand into a sponge, then into a cushion, then on the table.
flow.say: Press the sponge. Now the cushion. Now the table. Which pushes back with hardly any squashing?
flow.kid: Press a sponge. Press a cushion. Press the table. Which squashes least?

check.q: A book lies still on a table. Which forces are on it?
options: No forces, because it is still
Gravity pulling down, and the table pushing up just as hard
check.why: Gravity pulls the book down and the table pushes it up just as hard. Picking 'no forces' is very common. Still things have balanced forces, not no forces.

flow.do: Your child draws the book with two arrows of the same length, one down and one up.
flow.say: Draw gravity pulling the book down. Draw the table pushing it up. Same length or different?
flow.kid: Draw gravity pulling down. Draw the table pushing up. Make them the same length. They balance!
flow.think: If the floor stopped pushing up on you, where would gravity pull you?

activities.context: This activity uses a ruler bridged between two tins. It shows that a table pushes up on things resting on it, even though nothing seems to move.

activities.title: Forces From Far Away

materials.item: a bar magnet, or a strong round magnet. A flat, bendy fridge magnet is too weak for most of this.
a few steel paper clips
a sheet of paper and a thin book
a balloon
small torn bits of tissue paper
a ruler

activities.safety: Keep magnets away from phones, bank cards and very young children, who might swallow small ones.

schedule.what: Pull a clip with a magnet through paper and a book. Lift paper bits with a rubbed balloon. Drop things and watch gravity.

activities.record: Write how far away the clip jumped to the magnet. Then write whether the magnet could drag the clip through paper, a thin notebook and a thick book.

setup.art: A paper clip on a table, a magnet held above it near a ruler, the clip jumping up to the magnet.
setup.caption: 1. Move the magnet slowly closer to a clip. Measure when it jumps.

setup.art: A magnet under a sheet of paper, dragging a paper clip around on top.
setup.caption: 2. Put paper in between. Try again.

setup.art: A balloon rubbed on a child's hair, held over tiny bits of tissue paper that leap up to it.
setup.caption: 3. Rub a balloon on your hair. Hold it over paper bits.

flow.do: 1. Lay a clip on the table next to a ruler. 2. Move the magnet slowly towards it, and note how far away it is when the clip jumps. 3. Then put the clip on a sheet of paper and move the magnet underneath. 4. Try again with a thin notebook, then a thick book.
flow.say: The magnet hasn't touched the clip, but it jumped. What pulled it?
flow.kid: Move the magnet slowly towards the clip. When does it jump? Then try pulling it through paper and books.

ask.q: Did the paper stop the pull?
good: No, the pull went right through the paper.
Only the thick book stopped it, because it kept them too far apart.

flow.context: This is the first step of Forces From Far Away. You test pulls that work without touching.

flow.do: 1. Blow up the balloon and tie it. 2. Your child rubs it on their dry hair for 10 seconds. 3. They hold it just above the tissue bits.
flow.say: Rub the balloon on your hair. Hold it over the paper. What happens? Nothing touched the paper. What do you think pulled it?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon on your hair. Hold it over the paper bits. Watch them jump up!
flow.parent: After your child's guess: that is an electric force, working across a gap. Rubbing moves some electrons from the hair to the balloon. The balloon then attracts the paper. On a humid monsoon day it may not work well, because damp air carries the charge away. Try again in an air-conditioned room, or on a drier day.

flow.do: Drop a spoon, a ball and a crumpled paper from the same height.
flow.say: Nothing is touching these when they fall. What pulls them down?
flow.kid: Drop a spoon, a ball and some paper. Nothing touches them. What pulls them down?

check.q: Which of these is a force from far away?
options: The Earth pulling a falling spoon
check.why: Nothing touches a falling spoon, yet the Earth pulls it down. Picking the swing or the kick means touching forces were chosen. Those need contact.

flow.do: Look at the magnet results together.
flow.say: Look at the results. The paper didn't block the pull. Why did the thick book stop it?
flow.kid: Look at your results. Why did the thick book stop the pull?

chart.title: Made-up example results: can the magnet drag the clip through it?
cols: What was between the magnet and the clip
rows: A sheet of paper
Yes, easily
A thin notebook
Yes, slowly
A thick dictionary
No
chart.note: These results are made up. Your results will depend on your magnet.

flow.think: Gravity reaches all the way to the Moon. How can a pull cross empty space with nothing there?
flow.parent: Paper and books do not block a magnet's pull. A thick book just keeps the magnet too far away, and magnetic pulls get weaker quickly with distance.

activities.context: This activity tests three pulls that work without touching: a magnet, a rubbed balloon and the Earth's gravity.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: can the magnet drag the clip through it?
cols: What was between the magnet and the clip
rows: A sheet of paper
Yes, easily
A thin notebook
Yes, slowly
A thick dictionary
No
example_chart.note: These results are made up. Your results will depend on your magnet.

activities.title: Muscles Only Pull: build a cardboard arm

materials.item: two strips of thick cardboard, each about as long as a ruler
a paper fastener (split pin), or a short piece of string knotted through both holes
two pieces of string or two rubber bands
sticky tape

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the cardboard with a pencil point or a skewer.

schedule.what: Feel your arm muscles pull. Build a cardboard arm with two strings for muscles.

activities.record: Draw your cardboard arm bent and straight. Draw an arrow on the string that is pulling each time.

setup.art: A child's arm bending, a hand on the front of the upper arm feeling the muscle bunch up.
setup.caption: 1. Bend your arm. Feel the front muscle pull.

setup.art: Two cardboard strips joined at one end by a split pin, like an upper arm and a forearm.
setup.caption: 2. Join two cardboard strips with a split pin.

setup.art: Two strings running along the inside and outside edges of the cardboard arm, one pulled to bend it, one pulled to straighten it.
setup.caption: 3. Pull one string to bend. Pull the other to straighten.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts their left hand on the front of their right upper arm. 2. They bend and straighten the right elbow slowly. 3. Then they hold the back of the upper arm and do it again.
flow.say: Feel the front of your arm as you bend it. It gets fat and hard. That muscle is pulling. Now feel the back as you straighten.
flow.kid: Hold the front of your upper arm. Bend your elbow. Feel it bunch up? That muscle is pulling!
flow.context: This is the first step of the cardboard arm activity. You feel how your arm muscles pull, and then build a model.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes a hole near one end of each strip. 2. Join the strips through the holes so they bend like an elbow. 3. Tape the end of one string to the inside edge of the lower strip, near its middle. Lay it along the inside edge of the upper strip, under one loose loop of tape, so it can slide. 4. Tape the end of the other string to the outside edge of the lower strip, just past the elbow. Lay it along the outside edge of the upper strip, under a loose loop of tape.
flow.say: These two strings are the two muscles. Each one can only pull.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to make the holes. Join the strips with the split pin. Tape on two strings. They are your muscles.
flow.parent: It does not need to be neat. The inside string bends the arm when pulled. The outside string passes the back of the elbow and straightens it. Keep the loops of tape loose, so the strings can slide.

flow.do: Your child pulls the inside string to bend the arm, then the outside string to straighten it. Then they try pushing a string.
flow.say: Pull one string. Now pull the other. Now try to push the arm straight with the string.
flow.kid: Pull the inside string, and the arm bends. Pull the other, and it straightens. Can a string push?

check.q: Why do muscles work in pairs?
options: Because a muscle can only pull, never push
Because one muscle is always resting
check.why: A muscle can only pull, so it needs a partner to pull the other way. Picking 'muscles push and pull' is natural, but the string arm shows a string cannot push.

flow.do: Talk about other muscles.
flow.say: Your heart is a muscle too. It can only squeeze. But the squeeze pushes blood all round your body.
flow.kid: Your heart is a muscle. It can only squeeze. The squeeze pushes your blood around.
flow.think: If all your muscles only pull, how do you push a door open?
flow.parent: Good answer: muscles pull on bones, and the bones push the door. The bones work like levers, which you meet in the Simple machines unit.

activities.context: In this activity, you feel your arm muscles pull, then build a cardboard arm with two strings for muscles. It shows that muscles can only pull.

activities.title: Push and Pull Dance and Partner Yoga

materials.item: open floor space, a mat, and some music

activities.safety: Move slowly. Partners hold wrists, not fingers. Let go gently, never suddenly.

schedule.what: Dance pushes and pulls, then balance with a partner.

activities.record: Draw your favourite partner pose, with arrows for each pull or push.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up standing palm to palm, both leaning in a little, balanced.
setup.caption: 1. Push palms together. Lean in.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up holding wrists, both leaning back, balanced like a V.
setup.caption: 2. Hold wrists. Both lean back.

setup.art: Two children sitting facing each other, feet touching, holding hands, legs raised in a partner boat pose.
setup.caption: 3. Try a partner boat pose.

flow.do: Play music and call out a force. Your child dances it. Try a slow pull, a sudden push, a twist, and a pull from an invisible magnet.
flow.say: Dance a slow, heavy pull. Now a sudden push! Now a twist. Now be pulled by an invisible magnet.
flow.kid: Dance a slow pull. Now a sudden push! Now a twist. Now an invisible magnet pulls you.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Push and Pull Dance. You move your body like different forces.

flow.do: 1. Stand facing your child, palm to palm. Both lean in a little and push equally. 2. Then hold wrists and both lean back slowly.
flow.say: Push palms and lean in. If we push equally, we're balanced. Now hold wrists and lean back. Our pulls hold each other up.
flow.kid: Push palms and lean in. Now hold wrists and lean back. Your pulls hold each other up!

ask.q: What happens if one of us stops pushing?
good: The other one falls forward.
It is not balanced any more.

flow.do: Try a partner boat pose: sit facing each other, feet touching, hold hands, and slowly lift your legs together.
flow.say: Feet together. Hold hands. Pull a little and lift your legs. We only balance if we pull equally.
flow.kid: Sit facing each other with feet touching. Hold hands. Lift your legs slowly. Pull equally!

check.q: Two people lean back holding wrists, and stay still. Their pulls are…
check.why: Leaning back and staying still means the two pulls cancel, so they are balanced. Picking 'unbalanced' means you would both be falling one way.

flow.think: In the boat pose, which way does each of you pull? What would happen to your partner if you let go?

activities.context: This activity uses dance and partner yoga to feel pushes, pulls and balance with your whole body.

activities.title: Arrow Spotting: a day of forces

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil, or a phone to take photos

activities.safety: Outdoors only with a grown-up. Don't stand near traffic to take photos.

schedule.what: Spot six forces during the day. Draw each one with an arrow.

activities.record: Make a page of six small drawings or printed photos. On each one, draw an arrow for the force, and write what it is.

setup.art: A child sketching an auto-rickshaw being pushed by its driver, a big arrow behind it.
setup.caption: 1. Spot a push or a pull. Draw it, or take a photo.

setup.art: A sketchbook page with a drawing of a kite, an arrow drawn along its string.
setup.caption: 2. Draw an arrow on it. Start on the thing being pushed or pulled.

setup.art: A page of six small drawings with arrows of different lengths and labels.
setup.caption: 3. Make the arrow longer for a bigger force. Label it.

flow.do: Explain the job: spot six forces during the day, and draw each one with an arrow.
flow.say: Today you're a force spotter. Find six pushes or pulls. Draw each one, with an arrow.
flow.kid: You are a force spotter today! Find six pushes or pulls. Draw each one with an arrow.
flow.context: This is the first step of Arrow Spotting. You find forces during an ordinary day and draw them as arrows.

flow.do: During the day, help your child spot and draw six forces. Try a door, a swing, a cart, a kite, a broom and a falling leaf. Remind them of the three arrow rules.
flow.say: Remember the rules. Start the arrow on the thing. Point it the way of the force. Longer for a bigger force.
flow.kid: Start your arrow on the thing. Point it the way of the force. Make it longer for a bigger force.
flow.parent: Good finds include a vegetable seller pushing a cart and wind pushing washing on a line. A crane lifting is a pull. A falling leaf has gravity pulling it down and the air pushing it up.

flow.do: Look at the six drawings together.
flow.say: Which force was the biggest? Which drawing has the longest arrow?
flow.kid: Which force was biggest? Does it have your longest arrow?

check.q: You draw a gentle push and a hard push on a box. How should the arrows look?
options: The hard push has a longer arrow
The gentle push has a longer arrow
check.why: A bigger force gets a longer arrow. Picking 'the same length' means the arrow was seen only as a direction. It shows size too.

activities.context: This activity is a day of force spotting. You find pushes and pulls around you and draw each one as an arrow.

projects.title: Build a Balloon-Powered Car

materials.item: a small cardboard box or a piece of stiff card, about the size of your hand
4 bottle caps for wheels
2 wooden skewers for axles, or 2 empty ball-pen refills
3 drinking straws
a balloon
sticky tape and a rubber band
a measuring tape

projects.safety: Only a grown-up makes holes in the bottle caps and cuts skewers. Skewers have sharp points, so a grown-up snips the points off first.

schedule.what: Build the car body, axles and wheels. Fix on the balloon.
Race the car. Measure how far it goes. Improve it and race again.

projects.record: Draw your car with arrows: the air pushed backwards and the car pushed forwards. Write the distance before and after your improvement.

setup.art: A grown-up pushing a skewer through the middle of a bottle cap, with the sharp tip snipped off.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes holes in the caps for the wheels.

setup.art: A cardboard car body with two straws taped across the bottom and skewers through them, bottle caps on the ends.
setup.caption: 2. Tape two straws under the card. Push the axles through. Fix the wheels.

setup.art: A balloon taped over the end of a straw on top of the car, the straw pointing backwards.
setup.caption: 3. Tape a balloon to a straw. Tape it on top, pointing backwards.

setup.art: The car racing across a tiled floor, air rushing out of the straw behind it.
setup.caption: 4. Blow up the balloon through the straw. Let go!

flow.do: Remind your child of the balloon rocket. Ask how a balloon could push a car.
flow.say: Remember the balloon rocket on the string? It pushed air backwards, and the air pushed it forwards. Could a balloon push a car?
flow.kid: Remember the balloon rocket? Air went back, the balloon went forward. Can a balloon push a car?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Balloon-Powered Car project. You build a car that is pushed along by air rushing out of a balloon.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes a hole in the middle of each cap and snips the skewer points. 2. Tape two straws across the bottom of the card, one at each end. 3. Push a skewer through each straw. 4. Push a cap on each end of each skewer.
flow.say: The straws let the axles spin freely. Give the car a little push. Does it roll straight?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to make the holes. Tape the straws under the card. Push the skewers through. Add the wheels.
flow.parent: If the car does not roll, the axles may be rubbing. Make the straw holes wider, or check that the caps are pushed on straight.

flow.do: 1. Put the balloon's neck over one end of the third straw and fix it with a rubber band. 2. Tape the straw on top of the car, with the free end sticking out of the back.
flow.say: Which way must the straw point, so the car goes forwards?
flow.kid: Fix the balloon to a straw with a rubber band. Tape it on top. Point the straw out of the back.

check.q: The balloon car should go forwards. Which way must the air rush out?
check.why: The air must rush out backwards, so it pushes the car forwards. Picking 'forwards' would push the car backwards.

flow.wait: Leave the car somewhere safe until tomorrow.

flow.do: 1. Blow up the balloon through the straw. 2. Pinch the straw and put the car on the floor. 3. Let go. 4. Measure how far it went. 5. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Let go! How far did it go? What pushed it?
flow.kid: Blow up the balloon through the straw and pinch it. Put the car down. Let go! Measure how far it went.

chart.title: Made-up example: the balloon car before and after one improvement
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Choose one thing to improve. Change only that one thing. Race again and compare.
flow.say: Engineers improve one thing at a time. What will you change: the wheels, the balloon, or the straw?
flow.kid: Change one thing only. Wheels, balloon or straw? Race again. Did it go further?
flow.think: Real rockets carry their own gas to push out. Why can they work in space, where there is no air?

projects.context: In this 2-day project, you build a small car from card, bottle caps and skewers. A balloon on top pushes air backwards, and the air pushes the car forwards.

challenges.title: Move It Without Touching
challenges.problem: A ping-pong ball sits at one end of a table. Your job is to get it into a cup at the other end without touching it with your body.
constraints: You may not touch the ball with any part of your body.
You may not tip the table.
You may use anything from home, except a grown-up's hands.
materials: straws, a fan, a magazine to wave, a magnet, a balloon, string, tape, books
general: Blow on it through a straw, so your breath pushes it.
Wave a magazine to push air at it.
Build a slope with a book, so gravity pulls it down into the cup.
creative: Tape a steel paper clip to the ball. Then a magnet can pull it from far away.
Rub a balloon on your hair and use its electric pull to roll the ball.
Push a second ball into it, so one ball pushes the other.
Build a ramp with walls made of books. The walls push the ball and steer it.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it with arrows for every push and pull. Then try it.

setup.art: A ping-pong ball at one end of a table and a paper cup lying on its side at the other end.
setup.caption: 1. Put the ball at one end and the cup at the other.

setup.art: A child blowing through a straw, the ball rolling across the table.
setup.caption: 2. Try pushing it with air.

setup.art: A rubbed balloon held near the ball, the ball rolling towards it.
setup.caption: 3. Try a pull from far away.

flow.do: Set up the table. Read the problem and the rules together.
flow.say: You can't touch the ball. So how else can you push or pull it?
flow.kid: Get the ball into the cup. No touching! How can you push or pull it?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Move It Without Touching challenge. You must move a ball into a cup without touching it.

flow.do: Before trying anything, list three ideas. For each idea, say what pushes or pulls the ball.
flow.say: Engineers plan before they build. Tell me three ideas. What is the force in each?
flow.kid: Plan first. Draw three ideas. For each one, say what pushes or pulls the ball.

flow.do: Try each idea. Time how long each one takes to get the ball into the cup.
flow.say: Which idea worked best? Was it a touching force or a force from far away?
flow.kid: Try each idea. Which worked best? Did it touch the ball, or work from far away?

check.q: You blow on the ball through a straw. What pushes the ball?
options: Your breath, the moving air, pushes it
check.why: Your breath is moving air, and moving air pushes the ball. Picking 'nothing' misses that air is made of real particles, which can push.

flow.do: Read the usual and the creative ideas. Then invent a new one.
flow.say: Here are some other ideas. Can you invent one nobody has thought of?
flow.kid: Look at the other ideas. Now invent a brand-new way. Draw it with arrows.
flow.think: Air touches the ball when you blow. Is that a touching force or not?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must move a ping-pong ball across a table into a cup without touching it, using pushes and pulls of many kinds.

challenges.title: The Marble Bend
challenges.problem: Roll a marble from one corner of a tray so it turns a corner and ends in a cup at the other corner. You may only give it one push at the start.
constraints: Only one push, at the start.
The marble must turn at least one corner.
Use only books, card, tape and blocks to build the path.
materials: a large tray or a flat floor
books, strips of card, wooden blocks, tape
general: Put a book as a wall at the corner. When the marble hits it, the wall pushes it in a new direction.
Bend a strip of card into a curved wall, so it pushes the marble round gently.
Tilt the tray slightly so gravity keeps it rolling.
creative: Make the marble bounce off two walls, like a carrom coin off the edges of the board.
Use a second marble, waiting at the corner, to be hit and sent on.
If you have a steel ball instead of a marble, lay a magnet under the tray at the corner to pull it round.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your path from above. Draw an arrow at each place where something pushes the marble. Then build it and test it.

setup.art: A tray seen from above with a marble in the bottom-left corner and a cup in the top-right corner.
setup.caption: 1. Put the marble in one corner and the cup in the other.

setup.art: A book standing as a wall in the bottom-right corner, the marble's path drawn as a dotted line bouncing off it.
setup.caption: 2. Build walls to turn the marble.

setup.art: A child giving the marble one flick, the marble rolling, hitting the wall and turning towards the cup.
setup.caption: 3. Give one push. Watch it turn.

flow.do: Set up the tray, the marble and the cup. Read the problem.
flow.say: A rolling marble goes straight unless something pushes it sideways. How will you make it turn?
flow.kid: A rolling marble goes straight. What could push it round a corner?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Marble Bend challenge. You must make a rolling marble turn a corner using only walls you build.

flow.do: Your child draws the path from above, with an arrow for each wall's push.
flow.say: Draw your path first. At each wall, draw the wall's push on the marble. Which way does it point?
flow.kid: Draw your path from above. At each wall, draw an arrow for its push.
flow.parent: A wall pushes straight out from its surface. A marble hitting a wall at a slant bounces off at a slant, like a carrom coin.

flow.do: Build the path and test it. Change one wall at a time until it works.
flow.say: Try it. If it misses, move just one wall and try again.
flow.kid: Build it. Give one push. Did it work? Move one wall and try again.

check.q: A rolling marble hits a wall and turns. What changed its direction?
options: Its own speed made it turn
Nothing. It was always going to turn
check.why: The wall pushed the marble, and the push changed its direction. Picking 'its own speed' misses that speed alone keeps it going straight. It only turns when a force pushes it.

quiz.p: Which of these is a force?
quiz.why: A force is a push or a pull, and the magnet pulls. A colour or a length is something you can describe, but it does not push or pull anything.

quiz.p: A girl squeezes half a lemon over her rice. Is her squeeze a push or a pull?
quiz.why: Her fingers press on the lemon from both sides, so it is a push. Picking 'neither' means a squeeze was not seen as a force. But the juice comes out because she pushes.

quiz.p: A rolling ball reaches a rough doormat and stops. What stopped it?
opts: The mat rubbing against it, a force called friction
Nothing. It just ran out of moving
quiz.why: A moving thing only slows or stops if a force acts on it. Here it is friction, the grip between two surfaces. Picking 'ran out of moving' is a very old idea that turned out to be wrong.

quiz.p: Which of these needs no force at all?
opts: A ball rolling on at the same speed in empty space
quiz.why: Forces change motion. Starting and turning are changes, so they need a force. A ball going on at the same speed and in the same direction needs no force.

quiz.p: A football is kicked just as hard, once to the left and once to the right. Why does it end up in different places?
opts: The direction of the kick changed
quiz.why: Same strength means same size of force. Only the direction changed, and that alone sends the ball somewhere else.

quiz.p: Two girls blow on a ping-pong ball from opposite sides, equally hard. Predict what the ball does.
opts: It stays about where it is
quiz.why: Equal pushes in opposite directions balance. Picking 'slantwise' mixes this up with two pushes from a corner.

quiz.p: Where should a force arrow start?
opts: On the thing the force acts on
On the person doing the pushing
quiz.why: The arrow starts on the thing being pushed or pulled, and points the way the force goes. Picking 'on the person' draws the force on the wrong thing.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Both teams pull with 7. Which way will the rope move?
quiz.why: 7 and 7 are equal and opposite, so the pulls are balanced and the rope stays still. Picking left or right means one team was imagined as stronger.
quiz.context: In a tug of war, two teams pull a rope in opposite directions. The bigger total pull wins.

quiz.p: You jump from a small boat onto the shore. What happens to the boat?
opts: It moves backwards, away from the shore
It follows you to the shore
quiz.why: Your feet push the boat backwards as you jump, and the boat pushes you forwards. Picking 'stays still' means the push on the boat was forgotten.

quiz.p: A balloon car pushes air out of its back. What moves the car forwards?
opts: The air pushing back on the balloon
quiz.why: The balloon pushes the air backwards, and the air pushes the balloon, and the car, forwards. The wheels only help it roll.

quiz.p: A tug of war rope is pulled tight and is not moving. One end is pulled with 200 newtons. What is the pull at the other end?
quiz.why: A tight, still rope is pulled equally at both ends. Picking 400 means the two ends were added, but it is one pull passing along the rope.

quiz.p: Which force works across a gap, without touching?
opts: The Earth pulling a falling leaf
quiz.why: Gravity pulls from far away. The door and the ball need touching.

quiz.p: A balloon rubbed on your hair lifts tiny bits of paper without touching them. What kind of force is this?
opts: A pull from far away, an electric force
quiz.why: Rubbing gives the balloon an electric charge, which pulls the paper across a gap. Picking 'not a force' misses that the paper moved, and moving needs a force.

quiz.p: Muscles can only pull. So how do you kick a ball?
opts: Muscles pull on the leg bones, and the foot at the end pushes the ball
quiz.why: A muscle pulls on a bone, the bone swings, and the foot presses on the ball. A pull inside becomes a push outside.

quiz.p: You pull on the Earth too, just as hard as it pulls you. Why doesn't the Earth seem to move?
opts: It is so huge that the pull hardly moves it
You do not really pull it at all
quiz.why: The two pulls are the same size, but the Earth is enormous, so it moves far too little to notice. Picking 'you do not pull it' is the usual first guess.

quiz.p: Has the question 'what is a force, really?' been fully answered?
opts: No. Scientists still argue about it
quiz.why: Scientists can measure forces very exactly. But Newton, Einstein and physicists today give different answers to what a force really is.

applications: Engineers draw force arrows to design bridges, buildings, cranes and lifts, so nothing bends or falls.
Pilots and ship captains use arrows called vectors to add up the push of their engines and the push of the wind or the sea current.
Weather maps show the wind as arrows. India's weather forecasters use them to follow the monsoon.
Rockets, from Tipu Sultan's iron rockets to India's moon missions, move by pushing hot gas backwards.
Boats are rowed and poled by pushing water or the river bed backwards.
Doctors and physiotherapists study which muscles pull on which bones, to help people walk again after an injury.
Lifts, cranes and well buckets use ropes and cables, which can only pull.
Magnets pull and push in fridge doors, speakers, electric motors and some fast trains.
Sports coaches study pushes: a sprinter pushes the blocks backwards, and the blocks push the sprinter forwards.
Tug of war teams crouch low and push the ground, because the ground's push is what wins.
Solar sails let spacecraft be pushed through space by sunlight, with no fuel.
Video game designers use force arrows, called vectors, to make characters and balls move in a real way.

open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure forces almost perfectly. But whether a force is a real thing, a bend in space and time, or particles passing between things, is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Is gravity carried by a particle?
open_questions.why_open: The other basic forces are carried by particles. Many physicists think gravity is carried by a graviton, but nobody has found one. It may be far too weak to ever detect directly.

open_questions.q: How does a pull cross empty space?
open_questions.why_open: Newton refused to guess. Einstein said space itself bends. How that fits with quantum physics, the science of the very tiny, nobody yet knows.

open_questions.q: What is pushing the universe apart?
open_questions.why_open: In 1998, astronomers found that the universe is spreading out faster and faster. Something seems to push it apart. They call it dark energy, but nobody knows what it is.

open_questions.q: Are there only four basic forces?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists know of four: gravity, the electromagnetic force, and two inside atoms. Some experiments search for a fifth force. None has been confirmed.

open_questions.q: Why do the four forces have the strengths they do?
open_questions.why_open: Gravity is far, far weaker than the electric force. If the strengths were very different, stars and atoms might not exist. Nobody knows why they are what they are.

open_questions.q: How exactly do the tiny motor proteins in our cells pull their loads so well?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can watch them take steps. How thousands of them work together in a living cell is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the Arrow Wars game, you played arrows of 3 and 2. Your friend played arrows of 4 and 4. Which way does the rope move, and by how many squares?
maths.explain: Your total is 3 + 2 = 5. Your friend's total is 4 + 4 = 8. The pulls point opposite ways, so take the smaller from the bigger. 8 take away 5 is 3. Your friend's pull is bigger, so the rope moves 3 squares towards your friend.
maths.why_maths: Pulls the same way add up and opposite pulls take away, so adding and subtracting tells you which way a tug of war will go.
maths.context: Arrow Wars is this unit's card game about tug of war. Each card is an arrow, and its length is the size of a pull.

maths.problem: In the Push the Wall experiment, these were the three tries for a hard push: 90 cm, 110 cm and 100 cm. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the three numbers in order: 90, 100, 110. The middle one is 100. So the middle value is 100 cm. We use the middle value because one try can be a fluke.
maths.why_maths: Ordering your tries and picking the middle one gives a fair result, even if one try went wrong.
maths.context: In the Push the Wall experiment, you sit on a towel and push a wall with your feet, then measure how far you slid.

maths.problem: The balloon rocket went 90 cm with 3 breaths, 200 cm with 6 breaths and 300 cm with 9 breaths. Look at the chart. How much further did it go with 9 breaths than with 3 breaths?
maths.explain: 300 take away 90 is 210. So with 9 breaths, the balloon went 210 cm further than with 3 breaths. That is 2 metres and 10 centimetres.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which balloon went furthest, and subtracting tells you exactly by how much.

maths.problem: In Arrow Spotting, suppose you draw 1 centimetre of arrow for each unit of force. A push of 6 units and a push of 2 units act the same way on a cart. How long should the arrow for the total push be?
maths.explain: The pushes point the same way, so they add up. 6 + 2 = 8 units. At 1 centimetre for each unit, the arrow is 8 centimetres long. Measure it with a ruler, starting from zero.
maths.why_maths: Measuring arrows in centimetres makes the length show the size of the force exactly.
maths.context: In Arrow Spotting, you draw forces as arrows. A longer arrow means a bigger force.

maths.problem: In the Blow the Ball experiment, you blow from the bottom edge of the tray, and the ball rolls up. Then you move round a quarter turn and blow from the left edge. Which way does the ball roll now?
maths.explain: Blowing from the bottom pushes the ball up. Moving a quarter turn round to the left edge turns the push a quarter turn too, which is a right angle. A push from the left edge points to the right.
maths.why_maths: Turning a push through a quarter turn, a right angle, turns its direction, so angles help us say exactly where a pushed thing will go.
maths.context: In the Blow the Ball experiment, you blow on a ping-pong ball through a straw from different sides of a tray.

maths.problem: In the Gentle Tug of War, a child pulls with 4 units and a grown-up pulls the other way with 9 units. How much more must the child's team pull to make the forces balanced?
maths.explain: Balanced means both sides pull equally. The grown-up pulls 9. The child pulls 4. 4 + ? = 9. The missing number is 5, because 9 take away 4 is 5. So the child's team needs 5 more units, perhaps from a friend.
maths.why_maths: Finding the missing number tells you exactly how much extra pull would make the forces balance.
maths.context: In the Gentle Tug of War, a child and a grown-up pull opposite ends of a soft rope.

roots.context: We have been learning that every push and pull is a force, and that forces come in pairs. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Sitting on a towel, you pushed the wall with your feet and slid away from it. The wall pushed you back just as hard. You cannot move off by pushing on your own body. So to start moving, you, a bird or a rocket must push on something else.
deep_truth.habit: We say a person walks, or a rocket flies, by its own power, as if moving off needed nothing else. Every start needs something to push against: the floor, the water, the air or the rocket's own gas.
deep_truth.evidence: In Push the Wall, you moved only because you pushed the wall and the wall pushed you back. The balloon rocket went forwards only by pushing its air backwards.

three.who_am_i: Every time you push something, it pushes you back. You are never only the one who pushes.
three.what_is_life: Your muscles can only pull. Yet by pulling on your bones, they let you push, lift and hug.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth pulls you down, and you pull the Earth up just as hard. Every pull in the world has a partner like this.

roots.thread: Every force comes in a pair, acting on two different things. When you walk, you push the floor back, and the floor pushes you forward. Even the whole Earth moves back a tiny bit under your feet. This shows that no movement belongs to one thing alone: each step is shared between you and the ground. Science measures the sharing exactly, as two equal and opposite pushes.

teachings.teaching: Empedocles, a Greek thinker about 2,450 years ago, said two powers move everything. Love brings things together. Strife drives them apart.
teachings.link: Physics also finds that forces either attract, pulling things together, or repel, pushing them apart. Electrons repelling electrons is what makes every touching push.

teachings.teaching: All actions are done by the powers of nature. Only someone confused by pride thinks, 'I am the doer.'
teachings.link: The Gita is talking about who does our actions, not about physics. But this unit finds something close: you could not slide away from the wall by yourself. You moved only because the wall pushed back.

teachings.teaching: Think of the universe as one living being. All things in it act together and help cause everything that happens.
teachings.link: Every force is between two things, and everything pulls everything with gravity. No force ever acts on one thing only.

science.text: Every touching push you feel is the electrons in your hand and in the wall repelling each other.
Scientists can measure every force very well. But what a force really is, deep down, is still argued about.

other_view.view: A force pair is just a rule for how two separate things act on each other. It shows they affect each other. It does not show they are one, or that a step is truly shared.

how_we_found_out.who: Robert Goddard, an American rocket scientist, using Isaac Newton's rule that forces come in pairs
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people believed that a rocket needs air to push against. A swimmer pushes water and a bird pushes air, so people thought a rocket must push on something outside it too. In 1919, the American scientist Robert Goddard wrote that a rocket might one day reach the Moon. In January 1920, the newspaper The New York Times laughed at him. It said a rocket could not work in empty space, because there is nothing there to push against. Goddard had already tested this. He fired small rockets inside a closed container with most of the air pumped out. They still pushed forward, as well as in air or even better. The answer was a rule Isaac Newton wrote down in 1687: every push comes with an equal push back. A rocket pushes its own hot gas out backwards, and the gas pushes the rocket forwards. No outside air is needed. On 17 July 1969, as Apollo 11 flew towards the Moon, the newspaper printed a correction.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a rocket needs outside air to push against, so it could never work in empty space. Goddard's rockets pushed forward inside a container with the air pumped out.
